title: After Tome Hit 25 Million Users, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
dek: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he bets the CRM is won not by making salespeople do more work, but by whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
why: The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense, hands-on detail on pricing, expansion and org design.
who: Founders weighing a pivot or a product rebuild, product and pricing leads building AI-native SaaS, and investors thinking about the moat of systems of record.
skip: The first 0:00-2:01, the show trailer and guest intro, can be skipped; go straight to the main segment at 2:01.

points.h: They killed a hit not on the data, but on dislike
points.body: Tome launched alongside ChatGPT, reached 2 million users a month, and got so crowded that inference compute ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what actually made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a picky, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would write memos in it. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wouldn't close just by waiting for better models.

points.h: Follow the heat first, then find the real problem is data
points.body: The Tome team dug through its own user base, found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, and ran free pilots with 12 large companies. The original job was helping sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that heat, asked customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hard part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in those systems conflicts with itself. The reality in a call recording and the reality in the CRM often don't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

points.h: Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it
points.body: They started with a go-to-market assistant that AEs used daily but that they couldn't charge for — the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they shrank the team, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then discovered nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day and cared about enough to give feedback by the hour.

points.h: The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
points.body: Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth — eventually extending to what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. All the traditional CRM field updates and stage progression are triggered off that log, but underneath there is always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a lot of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from it.

points.h: Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fix it
points.body: They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send sales back in time to fill the data in — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schemaless" — connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it walks the activity log and backfills. Alex Rampell compressed this into "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

points.h: Someone used it to find frontier treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
points.body: Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from day one, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial subjects; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and hunting for frontier treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of "every ongoing clinical trial on earth," and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find a frontier treatment within days.

points.h: Win the founders and engineers first, wait for the sales VP to come around
points.body: Alex points out something often missed: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led capability free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. When that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

points.h: Pure per-seat and pure consumption pricing both blew up
points.body: They first tried pure per-seat pricing; acceptance was decent, but top users consumed 10,000 times what the tail did, which doesn't work long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits — and within three weeks nobody touched any feature. Keith calls it the company's worst three weeks: a pile of signups and no usage. Finally they split work into four categories: day-to-day CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there and it turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your site and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that one is health tech that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most untapped part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

points.h: No swim lanes — whoever's free takes the problem
points.body: Keith says Tome's biggest lesson was that "a lot of people were playing house": the product lead, the marketing lead and the CS lead each had their own swim lane, and got offended when someone commented on theirs, so the company crawled and couldn't pivot at all — a bunch of appendages not talking to the brain. Lightfield is the reverse: 40 people, no swim lanes, everyone owns both product and customer success, everyone joins the same standup every morning, the most important problems get ordered, and whoever's free — delivery, engineering, CS — takes it. They do continuous planning, with a list that can change daily and gets reassessed weekly. Because in this era anyone can get up to speed on a customer quickly through Lightfield, can pick up a design system library fast with an LLM, can auto-create tasks through Lightfield's Linear connection — so engineers, designers and CSMs all lead projects, and specialists just do more projects of the same kind.

points.h: Low bar to start a project, high bar to ship it
points.body: How do you stay aligned when everyone's a generalist? Keith's answer is a weekly roadmap and GTM meeting, and constant editing: a customer asks for this, how does it relate to the mission? It doesn't, so we don't do it. He describes it as continuous editing that keeps what the company puts out coherent. Paired with that are two bars: the bar to start a project at Lightfield is very low, but the bar to ship is very high — they still keep a company-wide bug bash, something Keith learned at Instagram: before a product goes to customers, the company itself has to like it first.

points.h: What makes him paranoid is speed, not competition
points.body: Keith says what worries him most is speed. He mentions reading a report about an a16z portfolio company that had been using some startup's CRM and moved to Salesforce because the startup couldn't build the dashboard they wanted in four months. That's what makes him most paranoid: Lightfield has a great wedge — being the best CRM for new companies — but it has to build everything, so those people never get the idea of going back to the old world.

points.h: In a red ocean you can only be an expansion company
points.body: Facing a world where anyone can prompt a product into existence, Keith says one skill Lightfield developed is reading an account's expansion potential. As a CRM company in a red ocean, they have to be an expansion company: in a fiercely competitive market you often don't get the initial land you expected, but by year three or year five that doesn't matter — you become an important part of the customer's company. So they prioritize by an account's three-year expansion value, favoring building for the fastest-growing customers rather than the average one, while admitting that at this stage you have to be "more extreme than usual" and build everything.

points.h: Silicon Valley is for logos, not for revenue
points.body: Keith says most systems-of-record companies ultimately get their real revenue scale from "more than 50 miles from here." He sees the Silicon Valley phase as a technique for collecting reference customers: some customers raised $200 million but have only three go-to-market people, yet they'll be huge later, so you do the work to perfection now and then take their logos to the rest of the world — "we have healthcare, we have fintech" — and then say we also serve a lot of great manufacturing companies and can now do the same for you. Alex adds the absurdity of the phenomenon: you store exactly the same thing, but because I sell toothbrushes and you sell Coca-Cola, I need to see whether my peers use it.

points.h: Big companies won't build the system, but they want to build the company brain
points.body: On DIY, Keith says it's slightly overstated: when the ICP was seed-stage founders, they'd often hear "I could pay you, or I could build it myself in four weekends," and their response was "good luck, call us in five weekends" — and the person would come back saying hallucinations, emails sent to the wrong people, everything wrong. But at bigger companies they don't hear "I'll build my own system of record"; they hear "I'll build my own company brain," and they hear it a lot. Many of those people come back later saying building a company brain or a business world model is genuinely hard, and the hardest part is probably modeling the customer — "we tried, we didn't like our own results, so now we're coming to you."

points.h: What excites him most is being the company's crystal ball
points.body: Keith says what excites him most is Lightfield becoming the crystal ball companies use for scenario planning: how many salespeople to hire, what product to build next, which way to go. He gives a customer example — a company selling to enterprises discovered in Lightfield that it needed a mid-market product, and built an entire new product line. Joe ties this back to Alex's point about "extremism": in an era when you can build anything, the answer is instead to have a tool like Lightfield and throw frontier intelligence at a genuinely complex decision — something that used to require very smart people, a lot of ops, SQL and a pile of other things, and now takes an afternoon or a weekend talking to Lightfield.

points.h: When you pivot, almost all the noise around you doesn't matter
points.body: Asked what advice he'd give his past self, Keith says the most important thing is: when you pivot, almost all the noise around you doesn't matter. You just need to find the pain point, be motivated to build a product or service that solves it, and focus on the customer almost obsessively — everything else is noise. He recalls the things he heard at the time — the office reminds people of the good old days, the food isn't inspiring enough, how will my options be repriced — and says none of it really mattered; put on blinders and stare at the core.

terms.def: A model of a company's reality, built from customer emails, calls and meetings, that AI agents can use directly.
Greenfield means serving brand-new companies not yet locked into existing software; brownfield means an incumbent-held market where customers are "hostage."
A predefined set of fields and table structures; Lightfield argues for no schema, inferring it afterward from the activity log.
Keith's word for the self-soothing judgment that "things will be fine once the next generation of models gets stronger."
Ideal customer profile — the type of customer a company should serve first.
